item.title: What the Tradwife Trend Reveals About the Psyche
item.description:
Identity

What the Tradwife Trend Reveals About the Psyche

Jungian view on why the tradwife movement evokes such powerful reactions.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • The tradwife debate expresses the father complex—both positively and negatively.
  • The tradwife identity can act as a persona that becomes an idealized social role, obscuring the real person.
  • Society’s reaction to tradwives reveals tensions in gender roles and longings for idealized solutions.

The tradwife trend is having a moment. Tradwives, or “traditional wives,” hold the belief that women should care for the household, while men should provide financially and make the family's decisions. From the runaway success of Caro Claire Burke’s tradwife book Yesteryear—with Anne Hathaway and Amazon MGM securing the movie rights nearly nine months before its official April release1—to the explosion of tradwife influencers and “wife school” programs, the tradwife movement is firmly part of the zeitgeist. Why?

In my last post, I explored how the father complex shapes the tradwife movement. Carl Jung described complexes as emotionally charged bundles of memories and experiences that cluster together around a core theme or archetype such as “father,” “mother,” or “wife.”

Shaped by personal, relational, and cultural experiences, complexes are universal psychological structures. They represent how our experiences become organized in the psyche around recurring human experiences and themes, influencing how we think, feel, and respond. You can read more about complexes in general here, the mother complex here, and the father complex here.

From a depth psychology perspective, the decision to become a tradwife or to desire a tradwife as a partner does not necessarily signify that a complex is driving the decision or reflect a “disorder.” Rather, it can be a healthy, conscious choice based on one’s values, personality, and real factors, such as one's economic situation. However, when the tradwife stance causes pain, suffering, impairment in functioning, or psychological problems, then it is a problem.

How the Father Complex Shapes the Tradwife Choice

Complexes are nuanced and don’t follow strict patterns, meaning a negative or positive father complex can explain the decision to become a tradwife. A negative father complex may support becoming a tradwife if one is unconsciously seeking the protection, security, or authority that was lacking with their father. Alternatively, a negative father complex may lead one to reject the role through defensive autonomy, achievement, and resistance to male authority.

A positive father complex may support the tradwife choice as an expression of trust in masculinity and family life. Conversely, it may also support a rejection of the tradwife role by encouraging individuation, leadership, and egalitarian relationships.

What’s also interesting is the polarization surrounding the tradwife movement. From the lens of complex theory, the polarization is unsurprising because a complex unconsciously compels us to take sides, often leading us to declare that one way of being is superior to another. We see this in the positive and negative comments about tradwives, and entire Reddit communities organized around tradwife influencers.

article continues after advertisement

The Power of Archetypal Images in the Tradwife Trend

The emotional charge around tradwives attests to the power and influence Jung ascribed to archetypal images. The tradwife trend in particular expresses cultural interest in archetypal feminine images such as motherhood, home, domesticity, relationships, caregiving, and nurturance.

On social media, tradwife influencers express archetypal images that resonate collectively—an “ideal” mother who bakes bread, engages in domestic rituals, and feeds her family from a garden, all while looking fulfilled and beautiful. These images harken to archetypal images of “home,” “hearth,” and “mother.” And it’s clear from all the commentary around tradwives and the tradwife trend that what Jungian psychoanalysts caution against has occurred: These images have led to inflation, dehumanization, idealization, and devaluation, and foster fantasy over living the contradictory realities of ordinary life.

The Hidden Realities Surrounding Tradwife Lifestyles

Because social media privileges carefully curated images, tradwives seldom reveal the challenges, tensions, or shadow side of their choice. The everyday messiness of family life is omitted—toddler tantrums and flour all over the kitchen floor, or painful realities such as marital affairs, family estrangement, and addiction.

As one tradwife patient shared with me, “My husband’s success gets more attention than my sourdough bread. I fool everyone with my cheerful face and avoid my husband. I am so resentful…but I can’t even imagine working, and I don’t want to give up what I have.” The tradwife can provide a ready-made, respected identity that becomes a persona that a woman identifies with, an idealized social role rather than a real person. This is exemplified in a New York Times piece published in June about tradwife influencer Hannah Neeleman, known as “Ballerina Farm” on social media, who opened a store in Utah.2

In the article, when asked about Neeleman and tradwives, Abbey Wood, 29, shared, “I live my whole life on a time clock,” so homemaking “has become a very big fantasy or a dream for me…It does seem like a luxury, too. Almost kind of fanciful, in this economy, in 2026.”

Wood echoes the perspective of many people attracted to the tradwife movement. When stressed about a job and an overbooked schedule, a bucolic, stay-at-home lifestyle becomes a fantasy, an imagined place where the stressors of daily life don’t exist. However, fantasies are just that, and this reality is as rife with conflicts, tradeoffs, and limitations as the lives of those who do not choose to be a tradwife.

article continues after advertisement

Still, it makes sense that Wood and others dream of a seemingly simpler, slower-paced lifestyle. When our culture celebrates certain kinds of achievement and equates busyness with virtue and success, the tradwife alternative can become compensatory, meaning it acts as a “corrective mechanism” that brings in what has been cut off. In other words, the tradwife movement could be restoring wholeness to a culture that has overvalued production and achievement while suppressing longings for home, family, connection, and simplicity that are at odds with success, mastery, and growth.

The Tradwife, the Self, and Our Culture

A central question is how being a tradwife is related to a woman’s Self. Is it a choice that expresses her individuation and development, or is it motivated by complexes and defenses? The answer will vary, and its impact will be unique to each woman. Yet these individual choices also shape our culture, influence broader cultural movements, and ultimately affect our collective lives, as the tradwife trend and the debate around it demonstrates.

item.title: The Question I Never Thought to Ask in the ER
item.description:
Depression

The Question I Never Thought to Ask in the ER

I spent years as an ER doctor, but one question changed how I think about crisis care.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Standard psychiatric assessments often miss what a patient is actually returning home to after discharge.
  • "What are you going home to?" surfaces critical information that rarely appears in charts or intake forms.
  • People in crisis seldom volunteer information that feels like a burden.
  • Understanding the post-discharge environment matters as much as stabilizing the acute crisis.

For most of my career in the ER, I was good at asking the right questions. When a patient presented with chest pain, I always asked, “When did it start? Does it radiate? Any cardiac history?” For overdoses, I would query: “What did you take? How much? When?” In a psychiatric crisis, I would investigate: “Are you safe? Do you have a plan to hurt yourself? Do you have access to means?”

All of those questions were automatic. They were the questions that would keep someone alive for the next couple hours.

What I wasn't asking, however, were questions about anything in the next week.

The Question That Changed Everything for Me

I don't remember exactly when I started asking it. But in my later years of practice—after enough patient follow-ups did not get made, and after enough patients came back through the same doors—I found a reason to start asking one more simple but meaningful question: "What are the circumstances you're going home to?"

Asking this direct, focused question changed how I understood my job. Some patients described a household full of people who had no involvement in what had just happened in the ER. Others reported they were going home to an empty apartment. One man told me his wife had left him three weeks earlier and he hadn't told anyone yet. One woman confided that her kids were with her mother and she wasn't sure their grandmother would bring them back if she found out why she was in the ER.

None of that was documented in a chart. Those details weren't likely to be mentioned in a brief routine assessment. Yet how they answered mattered enormously for what happened in the 48 hours after I discharged them.

What was missing?
Source: Image by WangXiNa on Magnific

When I went through my own depression, nobody asked me that question either. Nobody ever asked what I was going home to—probably because from the outside, it looked like the answer must have been something good.

I was still functioning at work, showing up to shifts, making decisions, keeping the professional mask alive. The people around me saw the facade for themselves: He's fine. He's working. He's Scott.

Yet they couldn't see that I was sitting in my car in the hospital driveway, or parked at home for 20 minutes, before I could make myself go inside. It often felt like there was a terrible distance between the front door and the couch that had to be negotiated as an act.

What the Answer to "What Are You Going Home to?" Reveals

article continues after advertisement

There is a key in that question. It doesn't just collect information; it signals to the person across from you that you're thinking past the clinical moment. It helps show that you understand this clinical moment isn't the whole picture. And if someone answers honestly, you can learn several things at once:

  1. Whether anyone knows what happened

  2. Whether the home environment is stable—not only physically safe, but emotionally as well

  3. Whether there's any support waiting for them or whether they're walking into a vacuum

  4. Whether the people at home are positioned to help or will likely make things harder

It also gives a person an opportunity to say something they might not have otherwise volunteered. People in crisis are often already embarrassed to be there. They don't offer information that feels like a burden or that seems irrelevant. A direct question opens a door for more conversation.

I started following it with a second question: "Does anyone at home know you're here?" The answer sometimes was yes, but sometimes no. Both answers told me something I needed to address before writing the discharge paperwork.

article continues after advertisement

If you're supporting someone through a crisis right now, ask them this type of question. Explore what they're walking back into, and listen to the answer. What they tell you will point towards where they need the most help in the coming days.

What question do you wish someone had asked you after a crisis?

item.title: Make No Mistake: Kratom is An Opioid
item.description:
Addiction

Make No Mistake: Kratom is An Opioid

It's often presented as benign or safe. In reality, kratom is fueling a rise in addiction.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Before the opioid epidemic became a public health crisis, multiple warning signs were misread or dismissed.
  • Tragically, a strikingly similar pattern seems to be emerging with kratom.
  • Kratom's main compound is an opioid that activates the same brain receptors as heroin and opioid painkillers.
  • The easy accessibility of kratom means the prevalence opioid use disorder is likely to keep increasing.

"Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it." —George Santayana

Long before the opioid epidemic became a full-on public health crisis in the U.S., there were multiple warning signs that were misread, minimized, and dismissed. Tragically, a similar phenomenon seems to be emerging with kratom.

Source: GOKALP ISCAN from Pixabay

In the late 1990s and early 2000s an unusual intersection of well-intentioned pain specialists and rapacious pharmaceutical companies combined to help create a body of scientific research that served to allay the traditional concerns about the addictive potential of prescription opioids. This involved a handful of small studies that purported to demonstrate the risks posed by opioids—including addiction—were minimal. That research was uncritically accepted by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), as well as by certain U.S. medical journals.

In response, state medical boards loosened their opioid prescribing standards, and the use of opioids was expanded to the treatment of a wide variety of chronic pain conditions. [1] This effectively precipitated the U.S. opioid epidemic, which led to the reemergence of much more widespread heroin use and the proliferation of synthesized fentanyl.

What Is Kratom and How Does It Relate to Other Opioids?

Kratom is the common term both for the dried leaves of the Mitragyna speciosa tree, native to Southeast Asia, and the drug made from them. Kratom contains more than 50 alkaloids (chemical compounds that often have pharmacological properties) and is currently sold legally online as well as at a variety of stores, including gas stations and convenience stores, in the form of capsules, powders, teas, and liquid shots.

Lower doses of kratom are associated with stimulant-like effects, while higher doses have opioid-like effects. Stimulant effects include alertness, rapid heart rate, and increased energy. Other effects can include relaxation, confusion, and pain relief similar to opioids and sedatives. People report using kratom to alleviate pain, to reduce the intensity of emotional discomfort, to decrease opioid or other substance use, and to manage both cravings and withdrawal symptoms related to opioids and other drugs.

According to the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s National Survey on Drug Use and Health, in 2024, an estimated 1.85 million Americans aged 12 and older used kratom, compared to 1.63 million in 2023. Past-year usage among adolescents aged 12–17 increased 51 percent from 43,000 to 65,000 over the same period. [2] Importantly, kratom products have not been demonstrated to be either safe or effective for any medical condition, and the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration has listed kratom as a “drug of concern” (even though kratom and kratom compounds are not listed on the U.S. schedule of controlled substances).

article continues after advertisement

Are We Doing Enough to Mitigate Kratom's Harms?

Earlier this month, the DEA announced a ban on a specific class of kratom products known as 7-OH, made by chemically treating kratom leaf to boost its opioid potency. This action is a step in the correct direction but does little to slow the broader public health problem, because ordinary kratom products will continue to remain legal and widely available in most states.

The opioid crisis in the U.S. was driven in large part by misleading promotion and aggressive marketing. The DEA’s limited action, in my view, reflects an acceptance of the kratom industry-created narrative that public health problems involving kratom are specific to products containing 7-OH, while the “ordinary” version is a natural nonaddictive wellness resource that enhances mood and relieves pain.

However, the reality of lived experience is substantially different. Kratom-related poisonings and hospitalizations rose 1,200 percent over the past decade,[3] and most of this increase predates the introduction of 7-OH products just two years ago. [4] In contrast to the DEA, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has long considered kratom itself (beyond 7-OH) to be dangerous.

In 2018, the FDA sought to classify kratom as a Schedule I controlled substance after concluding that the kratom leaf contains opioid compounds. Kratom industry lobbying helped stop that initiative, but the FDA website continues to warn Americans “not to use kratom because of the risk of serious adverse events, including liver toxicity, seizures, and substance use disorder.” [5]

That warning reflects the fundamental pharmacology of kratom: Its principal active compound is an opioid that activates the same brain receptors as heroin and prescription painkillers. Like other opioids, kratom can be highly addictive—repeated use leads to cravings, tolerance (the need for progressively higher doses), dependence, and withdrawal. As the FDA Commissioner put it unambiguously in 2018, kratom “isn’t just a plant, it’s an opioid.” [6]

article continues after advertisement

According to new research from the University of Michigan and Texas State University published in the Journal of Addiction Medicine, kratom use in the US is increasing, with the highest use at ages 21–34. Kratom use was shown to be strongly associated with cannabis use, preexisting DSM-5 substance use disorders, and serious psychological distress. [7]

As long as kratom remains so easily available, the number of Americans suffering from opioid use disorder is likely to keep rising and the opioid crisis will continue. We’ve seen this movie before: When a powerful drug becomes readily accessible and its addictive potential is denied or minimized, more people use it, the prevalence of opioid use disorder increases, and the adverse health and social consequences inevitably accumulate. As legendary baseball Hall of Famer Yogi Berra might have said, “It’s déjà vu all over again.”
